Healthcare Heroes

By: Laura Byrne | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We look beyond the bad news to celebrate those providing excellence against the odds in our crumbling healthcare system

Unique Selling Point:
It's common knowledge that South Africa's state healthcare system is hopelessly overburdened, under-resourced and dogged by inefficiency, corruption and maladministration. But in the midst of the mess, individuals and departments in our state hospitals are managing to serve their communities with integrity and true medical excellence. We take a look at two such departments.

Summary:
1. Dihlabeng Regional Hospital
Dihlabeng is a secondary hospital in Bethlehem, Free State. It receives patients referred from five district hospitals, and offers eight of nine basic services. It has 135 beds, averages 350 surgical operations monthly and serves about 3000 patients each month through its specialised clinics. In 2015, Carte Blanche highlighted the woes of Dihlabeng, which had only 5 medical officers running the hospital's nine departments. Doctors complained of a total lack of resources, a failure to appoint professionals to empty posts, and government's complete indifference. But clinical manager Dr Liam Selfridge paints a different picture. He aims for the hospital to be the best in the province, and says the excellence of the staff is attracting medical interns and community service doctors. He says most of his consultants have been there for at least 20 years, which provides the stability the hospital needs to succeed. They are working with government to improve services, and seeing success.

2. Chris Hani Baragwanath Speech Pathology Department
Dr Sadna Balton has headed up the Bara speech and hearing team since 1991, when it was a team of just six. Today she has grown it to a multidisciplinary team of over 40 specialists. The clinic has won multiple awards, and driven firsts including the first cochlear implant in a government hospital in 2006 - to date they have performed 180. It is the largest and most successful of its kind in the country. Most recently, the department has been recognised for its innovations during COVID-19: primarily telehealth programmes, which have improved patient attendance and therapy impact.

Further information:
1. Dihlabeng
The plan is to follow a surgical or orthopaedic intern through one afternoon and the following morning as they book a patient into the wards and then prep them for surgery. We will follow that patient through the journey, interviewing them pre and post op, and interview the surgeon (a consultant of 20 years) and a member of the nursing staff along the way. At each stage we will hopefully get an idea of what the hospital is doing right, and why it is a desirable location for interns and other staff alike. We will speak to clinical manager Dr William Selfridge about what the hospital is doing right, what has changed since 2015, and how he creates excellence in the government healthcare system.

2. Bara
The telehealth initiative was created to overcome the lockdown travel restrictions and allow patients to continue receiving care. The team partnered with an NGO to get Wifi access for patients in their homes or at free hotspots around Soweto, which had the added benefit of identifying numerous households for food assistance. They also raised money to provide the department with wifi. When restrictions eased, the telehealth initiative continued because the team saw the benefits: patients are able to receive therapy daily or weekly because they don't have to take a whole day off and travel. They can receive therapy in their own homes, where the suggestions, toys, etc are relevant. Attendance has improved and the team plans to keep the programme going. We will spend a day in the hospital, filming therapists as they interact both remotely and in-person with their patients to provide speech therapy. We will interview the therapists as well as a member of one of the patient support groups, which are self-run. We will then go to one of the patient's homes, to film the therapy from that side as well. This patient will probably be Baba Ndlovu, who has Parkinson's. The therapy programme he is enrolled in requires daily interactions with his therapist - an impossibility if he has to travel to Bara every day. Thanks to telehealth, he can now have daily therapy over video call. We will also interview Dr Balton about how she has grown the department over the two decades she has been there, and what makes for a successful therapy service in state healthcare.

Extra Budget Items:
Travel to Bethlehem and overnight stay for crew
Additional day with internal crew, no presenter, to pick up at-home interviews with patient.

UPSOUND: Derek Watts: Dumelang, Doctor!
Dr Fulufhelo Mudzwari: Lekae?
Derek: Lekae?
Fulu: Keteng lekae?
Derek: Busy day?
Fulu: Yes, busy day ahead of us today.

VO: State healthcare is too often a bad news story. But we’re seeking out professionals providing excellence against the odds. We’re at Dihlabeng Regional Hospital in Bethlehem.

UPSOUND: Dr Fulufhelo Mudzwari: Grade 9 is when I decided helping people, saving lives is what I want to do.

VO: We’re tagging along on the morning rounds with intern, Dr Fulufhelo Mudzwari.

UPSOUND: Fulu: Dumelang. Lekae?

LINK: Dihlabeng Regional Hospital takes referrals from five district hospitals and is a vital provider of specialised care in the province. But it hasn’t always featured in the media for positive reasons.

VO: In 2015, the hospital hit the headlines for medication stock-outs, dysfunctional infrastructure, and a desperate staff shortage that meant it couldn’t run a 24-hour service.

UPSOUND: Dr Liam Selfridge: We hit rock bottom and I think there was about four permanent doctors left, other than the specialists. And at that stage, I decided I don't want to leave it like this.

VO: Dr Liam Selfridge was appointed clinical manager in 2015. Since then, management has worked hard to pull the hospital back together.

UPSOUND: Dr Liam Selfridge: you don't lament. You don't say we don't have this, we don't have that. You say that I'm able to do this in spite of challenges rather than saying, I can't do this because of challenges.

UPSOUND: Matron Dimakatso Masheane: After 2015, everything changed.

VO: Acting head of nursing, Matron Dimakatso Masheane, has been at Dihlabeng for 22 years.

UPSOUND: Derek Watts: It was called the Hospital of Death.
Matron Masheane: Now, it's not hospital of death.
Derek Watts: Now you're getting compliments.
Matron Masheane: We really do get compliments as much as sometimes we do receive complaints, but which are being addressed immediately.

VO: And these patients awaiting surgery seem to agree.

UPSOUND: Derek Watts: The treatment here?
Mpuse: The treatment is very good.
Derek: So you’re in good hands.
Mpuse: I’m in good hands.

UPSOUND: Christoffel: A little bit nervous but I know Dr Vermaak is an excellent doctor.
Derek Watts: And what are the staff like?
Chris: Very helpful and sympathetic.

UPSOUND: Matron Masheane: We’re still challenged with the staff availability. But our staff having willingness to go as far as they can to reach the patients, I think that is the one that make me wake up in the morning and come.

VO: Dihlabeng now runs a full 24-hour service… and is a desirable location for young doctors in training.

UPSOUND: Dr Fulufhelo Mudzwari: They tell you that by the time you leave here, you're going to have enough like tools to go into the real world where you're a doctor on your own. And we see a lot of passion in this hospital.

UPSOUND: Dr Johann Vermaak: After 27 years, I'm still here because I think we can make a difference. We can help with the training of the junior doctors.
Derek Watts: That's what's kept you here.
Dr Vermaak: Ja. And I think I'll still be here until they chase me away when I have to retire.

VO: We’ve accompanied Dr Mudzwari into the operating theatre of Dr Johann Vermaak.

UPSOUND: Dr Vermaak: What the staff and the management of this hospital is doing, they're doing the best that they can with the financial constraints. We haven't got patients waiting longer than 3 to 4 weeks for an elective op. And I think that's not many state hospitals that can say that.
Derek Watts: Thanks Doctor, that was quite enlightening.
Vermaak: Thanks.

LINK: Derek Watts: You were doing a lot of work there.
Fulu: Not as much as the surgeon.
Derek: But you were doing well, Fulu. I’m not Dr Watts, but from what I’ve seen in this hospital when it comes to patient care, surgical procedures and the passion of all the healthcare workers, if other hospitals around the country could emulate this, I think we’d be pretty close to world class.

UPSOUND: Derek: You said in 2016 that you want this to be the best hospital in the Free State?
Dr Liam Selfridge: Everyone has their challenges. But Dihlabeng has stood out mainly for service delivery. Right across the board from surgery, anaesthesia, orthopaedics and internal medicine, every head of clinical unit has been here for more than ten years and some 20 years.

Dr Fulufhelo Mudzwari: We work around the challenges.
Derek Watts: So you wouldn't claim that the hospital is perfect?
Fulu: No, I would not say that it's a perfect hospital, but we are fighting to make sure that our patients are on top.

LINK: Well, that wraps up Dihlabeng Regional Hospital in Bethlehem and it was quite a surprise for us.

VO: Next we’re headed to Chris Hani Baragwanath Hospital in Soweto, to focus not on frontline medicine, but rehabilitation.

UPSOUND: Dr Sadna Balton: It's not just about saving lives. It's also about the quality of lives once they're discharged from hospital.

VO: Dr Sadna Balton has headed the Speech Therapy and Audiology Department since 2001. It’s been recognised for many innovations, including the first cochlear implant in a state facility, in 2006.

UPSOUND: Dr Balton: When we reach a hurdle and when we’re told something can't happen, we look at how else can we make this happen?

VO: More recently, the pandemic lockdowns sparked another innovation.

UPSOUND: Dani Schlesinger: Telehealth has existed in the world for some time. And so what that means is it's been possible to see a family or a patient who is not with you virtually. But up until then, that had been not been permitted for us.

VO: Dani Schlesinger coordinates the cochlear implant team.

UPSOUND: Derek Watts: But surely a lot of your patients don't have the latest laptops and tablets?
Dani Schlesinger: The first thing that we did was we contacted all of our patients, to say, what do you have available? And then we catered an individualised telehealth plan for each patient based on the technology that they had available.

VO: Although lockdowns have ended, the majority of Katia Sarris’s patients still choose telehealth.

UPSOUND: Katia Sarris: We get siblings to join in on sessions and uncles and aunts to join in on sessions. You're doing therapy with them in real time in their environment.

UPSOUND: Katia Sarris: How are you? That’s good!

VO: Keamogetse Tshabalala relies on one cochlear implant and a hearing aid. Telehealth makes life a little easier for her mom Sindi.

UPSOUND: Sindi Tshabalala: When she comes from school, the department is closed at the hospital, but her speech therapist will go an extra mile and do after hours. I don’t need to be absent at work to take her to the speech, so I can do it at the comfort of our own home.

UPSOUND: Sindi Tshabalala: Say high five to your sister, she’s doing fine!

UPSOUND: Katia Sarris: Because you're not there, the ownership goes straight onto the parents. So you’re actually counselling the parent on what to do and they're learning the skills.

VO: Both patient attendance and outcomes have improved dramatically.

UPSOUND: Dani Schlesinger: Our goal was to find a substitute for therapy when someone can’t come in. And I think what we've realised is that, in fact, we've really been able to offer a much richer package with it.

LINK: Covid-19 compounded many of the challenges we face in this country, like unemployment and access to basic healthcare. But it also sparked life-changing innovation.

UPSOUND: Sindi Tshabalala: Their services, they are out of this world. They are above the private facility. Sometimes you need not to listen to stories. You need to go there yourself.

UPSOUND: Dr Balton: I’m working at a hospital because my patients have a right to the best. There should never be this thing that, comparing ourselves to private healthcare. Because for me, that is not the benchmark. The benchmark is actually what our patients are saying to us about the services they get.

VO: It can be hard not to believe that the challenges in our healthcare system are insurmountable. But perseverance, passion, and strong leadership really can produce excellence.



PROMO 1 (21 SECS)
VO: State healthcare in South Africa has a poor reputation.
UPSOUND: Sindi Tshabalala: I said I’m not going to a public hospital, because I heard stories.
VO: But we’re seeking out the places where passion and perseverance are producing excellence.
UPSOUND: Dr Sadna Balton: I’m working at a hospital because my patients have a right to the best.
UPSOUND: Sindi Tshabalala: Their services, they are out of this world.


PROMO 2 (21 SECS)
LINK: It was called the hospital of death…
UPSOUND: Dr Liam Selfridge: We hit rock bottom. And at that stage, I decided I don't want to leave it like this.
Seven years later, students are fighting to work there.
UPSOUND: Dr Fulufhelo Mudzwari: A lot of people in my class wanted to come here.
LINK: Is the blueprint for improved healthcare hidden in Bethlehem?


PROMO 3 (11 SECS)
LINK: State healthcare gets a bad rap in South Africa – often for a good reason. We’re seeking out the hospitals that do the best they can, with the resources they have, to care for their patients.

I don’t need to be absent at work to take her to the speech, so I can do it at the comfort of our own home. UPSOUND: Sindi Tshabalala: Say high five to your sister, she’s doing fine! VO: Both patient attendance and outcomes have improved dramatically. UPSOUND: Dani Schlesinger: Our goal was to find a substitute for therapy when someone can’t come in. And I think what we've realised is that, in fact, we've really been able to offer a much richer package with it. LINK: Covid-19 compounded many of the challenges we face in this country, like unemployment and access to basic healthcare. But it also sparked life-changing innovation. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We look beyond the bad news to celebrate those providing excellence against the odds in our crumbling healthcare system
metadata.Unique Selling Point: It's common knowledge that South Africa's state healthcare system is hopelessly overburdened, under-resourced and dogged by inefficiency, corruption and maladministration. But in the midst of the mess, individuals and departments in our state hospitals are managing to serve their communities with integrity and true medical excellence. We take a look at two such departments.
metadata.Summary: 1. Dihlabeng Regional Hospital Dihlabeng is a secondary hospital in Bethlehem, Free State. It receives patients referred from five district hospitals, and offers eight of nine basic services. It has 135 beds, averages 350 surgical operations monthly and serves about 3000 patients each month through its specialised clinics. In 2015, Carte Blanche highlighted the woes of Dihlabeng, which had only 5 medical officers running the hospital's nine departments. Doctors complained of a total lack of resources, a failure to appoint professionals to empty posts, and government's complete indifference. But clinical manager Dr Liam Selfridge paints a different picture. He aims for the hospital to be the best in the province, and says the excellence of the staff is attracting medical interns and community service doctors. He says most of his consultants have been there for at least 20 years, which provides the stability the hospital needs to succeed. They are working with government to improve services, and seeing success. 2. Chris Hani Baragwanath Speech Pathology Department Dr Sadna Balton has headed up the Bara speech and hearing team since 1991, when it was a team of just six. Today she has grown it to a multidisciplinary team of over 40 specialists. The clinic has won multiple awards, and driven firsts including the first cochlear implant in a government hospital in 2006 - to date they have performed 180. It is the largest and most successful of its kind in the country. Most recently, the department has been recognised for its innovations during COVID-19: primarily telehealth programmes, which have improved patient attendance and therapy impact.
metadata.Further information: 1. Dihlabeng The plan is to follow a surgical or orthopaedic intern through one afternoon and the following morning as they book a patient into the wards and then prep them for surgery. We will follow that patient through the journey, interviewing them pre and post op, and interview the surgeon (a consultant of 20 years) and a member of the nursing staff along the way. At each stage we will hopefully get an idea of what the hospital is doing right, and why it is a desirable location for interns and other staff alike. We will speak to clinical manager Dr William Selfridge about what the hospital is doing right, what has changed since 2015, and how he creates excellence in the government healthcare system. 2. Bara The telehealth initiative was created to overcome the lockdown travel restrictions and allow patients to continue receiving care. The team partnered with an NGO to get Wifi access for patients in their homes or at free hotspots around Soweto, which had the added benefit of identifying numerous households for food assistance. They also raised money to provide the department with wifi. When restrictions eased, the telehealth initiative continued because the team saw the benefits: patients are able to receive therapy daily or weekly because they don't have to take a whole day off and travel. They can receive therapy in their own homes, where the suggestions, toys, etc are relevant. Attendance has improved and the team plans to keep the programme going. We will spend a day in the hospital, filming therapists as they interact both remotely and in-person with their patients to provide speech therapy. We will interview the therapists as well as a member of one of the patient support groups, which are self-run. We will then go to one of the patient's homes, to film the therapy from that side as well. This patient will probably be Baba Ndlovu, who has Parkinson's. The therapy programme he is enrolled in requires daily interactions with his therapist - an impossibility if he has to travel to Bara every day. Thanks to telehealth, he can now have daily therapy over video call. We will also interview Dr Balton about how she has grown the department over the two decades she has been there, and what makes for a successful therapy service in state healthcare.
